newsitem.title: USA: Official declares Teamsters chief Carey re-elected.
newsitem.headline: Official declares Teamsters chief Carey re-elected.

text.p: Teamsters Union President Ron Carey was officially declared the winner on Friday in his hard fought re-election bid against rival James Hoffa for the leadership of the 1.4 million-member union.

Court-appointed Election Officer Barbara Zack Quindel declared Carey the winner exactly one month after the onset of a protracted ballot-counting process, as his margin over Hoffa exceeded the number of ballots that are still unprocessed.
Carey drew 233,369 votes, or 51.71 percent of the total, against Hoffa's 217,802, or 48.28 percent out of a total of 456,707 mail-in ballots counted, Quindel reported.

Since Carey's victory margin exceeded the 12,956 unprocessed "challenged ballots" -- those that were set aside last month for eligibility checks -- Hoffa could not possibly win the race, according to the election officer.
Carey's margin, while narrow, also exceeded the 3 percentage-point trigger, below which an automatic recount would have been required.

Carey, 60, never trailed in the balloting and last month declared himself the winner over Hoffa, 55, the son and namesake of the legendary Jimmy Hoffa who ruled the International Brotherhood of Teamsters in the 1950s and 1960s and is presumed to have been murdered by the mob in 1975.

Carey, who won the Teamster presidency as a reform candidate in the union's first open election five years ago, had fought a rough-and-tumble battle against Hoffa, whom he has accused of being backed by the mob and Teamster employers.
The election, only the second in the union's 93-year history, was required to be government-supervised and open to rank-and-file members under a 1989 settlement of a federal anti-racketeering suit.

Hoffa, a Detroit labor lawyer who has worked for the past three years for a Teamster joint council that was once headed by his father, has filed several protests that accused the election officer of a variety of irregularities.
"We've been very troubled by the processing of the challenged ballots," said Hoffa spokesman Richard Leebove. "Quindel and her cronies have picked which ballots are eligible."

By selecting which of the challenged ballots to process without election observers present, the officials could manipulate the results to ensure that Carey's margin exceeds the 3 percent recount trigger, Leebove said.
Quindel also has come under fire for what first appeared to be a shortfall of more than 25,000 ballots below the number that postal authorities said they delivered to her office.

Last week she explained the discrepancy, saying the larger number was the result of double-counting errors by her staff and the U.S. Postal Service. She denied that any ballots were missing and declared her counting procedures sound.

Responding to a request by Hoffa, U.S. Attorney Mary Jo White said last week that the Justice Department and Federal Bureau of Investigation "are closely reviewing and monitoring" the matter. Two lawmakers also have asked Attorney General Janet Reno to review the election.
